¶
'''wreche†''', ''n.'' See ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wreck'''<sup>1</sup> (rek), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wrak'', ''wrek'', ''wrec'', < AS. ''wræc'', expulsion, banishment, exile, misery (= D. ''wrak'', wreck, = Icel. ''rek'' (for ''vrek''), also ''reki'', anything drifted or driven ashore, = Sw. ''vrak'', refuse, trash, wreck, = Dan. ''vrag'', wreck), < ''wrecan'' = Icel. ''reka'', etc., drive: see ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''wrack''<sup>1</sup>, a doublet of ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The destruction, disorganization, disruption, or ruin of anything by force and violence; dilapidation: as, the ''wreck'' of a bridge; the ''wreck'' of one’s fortunes.
{{smaller block|Hence grew the general ''wreck'' and massacre.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 1. 135.}}
The ''wreck'' of matter and the crush of worlds.
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is in a state of wreck or ruin, or remains from the operation of any destroying agency: as, the building is a mere ''wreck''; he is but the ''wreck'' of his former self.
{{smaller block|But still the brave old soul held on, making the most of the ''wreck'' of life, now drifting alone to the Islands of the Blessed. ''Theodore Parker'', Historic Americans, vi.
<poem>Naught remains the saddening tale to tell,
Save home’s last ''wrecks''—the cellar and the well!</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Island Ruin.}}}}
'''3.''' The partial or total destruction of a vessel at sea or in any navigable water, by any accident of navigation or by the force of the elements; shipwreck.
{{smaller block|<poem>Go, go, begone, to save your ship from ''wreck'',
Which cannot perish, having thee on board.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 1. 156.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wreath|6988|'''wrecker'''}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|<poem>With bruised arms and ''wreaths'' of victory.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 110.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>[He] afterward attain’d
The royal Scottish ''wreath'', upholding it in state.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, v. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>With ''wreaths'' of grace he crowns my conquering brows.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A lute she held; and on her head was seen
A ''wreath'' of roses red, and myrtles green.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 1128.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Round the sufferer’s temples bind
''Wreaths'' that endure affliction’s heaviest shower,
And do not shrink from sorrow’s keenest wind.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}}
'''2.''' In ''her.'': (''a'') A garland or diadem for the head. {{smaller|(1) A chaplet of flowers or leaves, the general character being described in the blazon. (2) A sort of twist or heavy cord composed of the chief color and the chief metal in the achievement. It is not often used as a bearing, but is placed upon or above the helmet to receive the crest. It is then shown edgewise, and resembles a short piece of stout rope, and should show three turns of the metal and three of the color, beginning at the dexter side with the metal. Such a wreath may also be borne on the head of a man or a woman. It is then represented in perspective as in nature.}} (''b'') The tail of a wild boar: mentioned in the blazon only when of a different tincture from the rest of the bearing.—'''3.''' Something resembling a twisted band; something narrow, long, and circular, of slightly irregular outline.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Clouds began
To darken all the hill, and smoke to roll
In dusky ''wreaths.''
</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 58.}}}}

[[File:century v08 p0792 c1f1.png|center|218px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Wreath, as worn at the end of the 14th century: the origin of the heraldic wreath borne under the crest and seeming to support it. (From Viollet-le-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>As ''wreath'' of snow, on mountain-breast,
Slides from the rock that gave it rest.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., vi. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''wreath'' of airy dancers hand-in-hand
Swung round the lighted lantern of the hall.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Guinevere.}}}}
'''4.''' A defect in glass, consisting of a wavy appearance, due to want of uniform density. This defect is most common in flint-glass.—'''5.''' The {{img float|file=century v08 p0792 c1f2.png|width=93px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Wreath Circular.}}}} trochal disk of a rotifer with its fringe of cilia. See cuts under ''Rotifera'' and ''trochal''.—'''Civic wreath.''' {{smaller|See ''civic''.}}—'''Purple wreath.''' {{smaller|See ''Petrea''.}}—'''St. Peter’s wreath.''' {{smaller|Same as ''Italian may'' (which see, under ''may''<sup>4</sup>).}}—'''Wreath circular,''' {{smaller|in ''her.'', a wreath shown fully, not edgewise or in perspective, forming, therefore, a complete circle. It is in this form that a wreath is generally shown when used as a bearing.}}

'''wreath,''' ''v.'' See ''wreathe''.

'''wreath-animalcule''' (rēth′an-i-mal″kūl), ''n.'' An animalcule of the family ''Peridiniidæ''.

'''wreathe''' (rēᴛ̵ʜ), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wreathed'' (pp. also ''wreathen''), ppr. ''wreathing''.   [Also ''wreath''; < ME. ''wrethen''; < ''wreath'', ''n''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To twist; form by twisting.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of them the shepheard which hath charge in chief
Is Triton, blowing loud his ''wreathed'' horne.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Colin Clout, l. 245.}}}}
{{smaller block|Two chains of pure gold . . . of ''wreathen'' work.
{{right|Ex. xxviii. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>An adder
''Wreathed'' up in fatal folds.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 879.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And in the arm’d ship, with a well-''wreath’d'' cord,
They straitly bound me. ''Chapman'', Odyssey, xiv. 485.</poem>}}

{{smaller block|They killed a man which was a first-borne, ''wreathing'' his head from his bodie, and embalming the same with salt and spices. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 137.}}}}
'''2†.''' To writhe; contort; distort.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then walks off melancholic, and stands ''wreathed'',
As he were pinned up to the arras, thus.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Impatient of the wound,
He rolls and ''wreathes'' his shining body round.</poem>
{{right|''Gay'', Rural Sports, i.}}}}
'''3.''' To form into a wreath; adjust as a wreath or circularly; cause to pass about something. {{smaller block|<poem>About his neck
A green and gilded snake had ''wreathed'' itself.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 3. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then he found a door
And darkling felt the sculptured ornament
That ''wreathen'' round it made it seem his own.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}
'''4.''' To form or make by intertwining; also, to twist together or intertwine; combine, as several things into one, by twisting and intertwining.
{{smaller block|<poem>From his slack hand the garland ''wreathed'' for Eve
Down dropp’d.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 892.}}}}
'''5.''' To surround with a wreath or with anything twisted or twined; infold; twist, twine, or fold round.
{{smaller block|Each ''wreathed'' in the other’s arms.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Dusk faces with white silken turbans ''wreathed''.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 76.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And with thy winding ivy ''wreathes'' her lance.</poem>{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vii. 549.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wreathed'' in smoke the ship stood out to sea.</poem>{{right|''M. Arnold'', Balder Dead, iii.}}}}
'''6.''' To form or become a wreath about; encircle.
{{smaller block|<poem>In the Flow’rs that ''wreathe'' the sparkling Bowl
Fell Adders hiss.</poem>{{right|''Prior'', Solomon, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Wreathed column''', in ''arch.'', a column so shaped as to present a twisted or spiral form.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To take the form of a wreath; hence, to mingle or interlace, as two or more things with one another.
{{smaller block|<poem>A bow’r
Of ''wreathing'' trees.</poem> {{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Eclogues, ix. 85.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''milling'', to hug the eye of the millstone so closely as to retard or prevent its descent: said of flour or meal.

'''wreathen''' (rē′ᴛ̵ʜn), ''p. a.''   [< ME. ''wrethen'', var. of ''writhen'', pp. of ''writhe'': see ''writhen''. In present use ''wreathen'' is regarded as a poetical form for ''wreathed'', pp. of ''wreathe'', ''v.'']   Wreathed; twisted; specifically, in ''her.'', having many coils or circular curves, as a serpent when the body is coiled in different parts of its length.
{{smaller block|<poem>The hegge also . . .
With sicamour was set and eglatere
''Wrethen'' in fere so wel and cunningly.</poem>
{{right|''Flower and Leaf'', l. 57.}}}}

'''wreather''' (rē′ᴛ̵ʜėr), ''n.'' One who or that which wreathes, twists, or twines.
{{smaller block|''Wreather'' of poppy buds and weeping willows!
{{right|''Keats'', Sleep and Poetry.}}}}

'''wreath-shell''' (rēth′shel), ''n.'' Any member of the ''Turbinidæ'', and especially of the genus ''Turbo''. {{smaller|The species are numerous, and some of them highly ornamental when polished. See cuts under ''Turbo, Imperator'', and ''operculum''.}}

'''wreathy''' (rē′thi), ''a.''   [< ''wreath'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Twisted; curled; spiral.   ''Sir T. Browne.''—'''2.''' Surrounded or decked with a wreath or with something resembling a wreath.
{{smaller block|Shake the ''wreathy'' spear. {{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, iv. 438.}}}}

'''wrecche†''', '''wrecched†'''. Middle English forms of ''wretch'', ''wretched''.

'''wreche†''', ''n.'' See ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wreck'''<sup>1</sup> (rek), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wrak'', ''wrek'', ''wrec'', < AS. ''wræc'', expulsion, banishment, exile, misery (= D. ''wrak'', wreck, = Icel. ''rek'' (for ''vrek''), also ''reki'', anything drifted or driven ashore, = Sw. ''vrak'', refuse, trash, wreck, = Dan. ''vrag'', wreck), < ''wrecan'' = Icel. ''reka'', etc., drive: see ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''wrack''<sup>1</sup>, a doublet of ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The destruction, disorganization, disruption, or ruin of anything by force and violence; dilapidation: as, the ''wreck'' of a bridge; the ''wreck'' of one’s fortunes.
{{smaller block|Hence grew the general ''wreck'' and massacre.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 1. 135.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''wreck'' of matter and the crush of worlds.
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is in a state of wreck or ruin, or remains from the operation of any destroying agency: as, the building is a mere ''wreck''; he is but the ''wreck'' of his former self.
{{smaller block|But still the brave old soul held on, making the most of the ''wreck'' of life, now drifting alone to the Islands of the Blessed. ''Theodore Parker'', Historic Americans, vi.
<poem>Naught remains the saddening tale to tell,
Save home’s last ''wrecks''—the cellar and the well!</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Island Ruin.}}}}
'''3.''' The partial or total destruction of a vessel at sea or in any navigable water, by any accident of navigation or by the force of the elements; shipwreck.
{{smaller block|<poem>Go, go, begone, to save your ship from ''wreck'',
Which cannot perish, having thee on board.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 1. 156.}}}}

'''4.''' A vessel ruined by wreck; the hulk and spars, more or less dismembered and shattered, of a vessel cast away or completely disabled by breaching, staving, or otherwise breaking.
{{smaller block|In the statute of Westminster the first [3 Edw. I., c. 4], the time of limitation of claims given by the charter of Henry II. is extended to a year and a day, . . . and it enacts that, if a man, a dog, or a cat escape alive, the vessel shall not be adjudged a ''wreck''. {{right|''Blackstone'', Com., I. viii.}}}}

'''5.''' That which is cast ashore by the sea; shipwrecked property, whether a part of the ship or of the cargo; wreckage; in ''old Eng. common law'', derelict of the sea cast upon land within the body of a country, and not in the possession of the owner or his agents. {{smaller|''Wreck'', or more fully ''wreck of the sea'', was at common law applied only to wrecked property cast by the sea upon the land; and this included things grounded—that is, not floating at the time of seizure, although in a position where the tide would float them again. All such property was originally the perquisite of the crown, or of its tenant the lord of the manor; but in course of time an exception was made of wrecks from which any living thing escaped to land, in which case a presumption that an owner would appear arose and the property was preserved for a year and a day, after which if no claim was established the right of the crown was recognized. Wrecked matter floating was within the jurisdiction not of the common-law courts, but of admiralty, and known as ''derelict'', or ''derelict of the sea''. This too was a perquisite of the crown, claimed under the name of a ''droit of admiralty''. Such matter was classed as ''flotsam'', ''jetsam'', and ''lagan'' or ''ligan'' (which see). In the United States the right to derelict for which the owner does not appear is in the Federal government; the right to wreck for which he does not appear is in the State to whose coast it comes, subject usually in either case to the right of the rescuer of it to a compensation known as ''salvage''.}}

'''6.''' Seaweeds cast ashore by storms; wrack.—'''Commissioners of wrecks''' (in Maine, Massachusetts, {{smaller|and Rhode Island), '''receivers of wrecks''' (in Great Britain), '''wreck-masters''' (in New York and Texas), officers whose duty it is to take charge of wrecked property on the part of the coast for which they are appointed, and preserve it for the owner, or, if unclaimed, for the state.—'''Wreck commissioner,''' in Great Britain, one of a tribunal consisting of not more than three, appointed by the lord chancellor, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1876 (39 and 40 Vict., c. 80), for the purpose of investigating shipping casualties.}}

'''wreck<sup>1</sup>''' (rek), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wrecked'', ppr. ''wrecking''.   [< ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause the wreck of, as a vessel; suffer to be ruined or destroyed in the course of navigation or management: said specifically of the person under whose charge a vessel is at the time of its wreck, and usually implying blame, even in case of misfortune.
{{smaller block|<poem>Friends, this frail bark of ours, when sorely tried,
May ''wreck'' itself without the pilot’s guilt,
Without the captain’s knowledge.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}
'''2.''' To cause the downfall or overthrow of; ruin; shatter; destroy; bring into a disabled or ruinous condition by any means: as, to ''wreck'' a railroad-train or a bank; to ''wreck'' the fortunes of a family.
{{smaller block|<poem>Weak and envy’d, if they should conspire
They ''wreck'' themselves, and he hath his desire.</poem>
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, iii. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|The meeting-houses of the Dissenters were everywhere ''wrecked''. {{right|''Lecky'', Eng. in 18th Cent., i.}}}}
'''3.''' To involve in a wreck; imperil or damage by wreck: as, a ''wrecked'' sailor; ''wrecked'' cargo.
{{smaller block|<poem>Here I have a pilot’s thumb,
''Wreck’d'' as homeward he did come.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 3. 29.}}}}

{{smaller block|The spurious tea-men are also the buyers of ''wrecked'' tea—that is, of tea which has been part of the salvage of a ''wrecked'' vessel.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 151.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Like golden ripples hasting to the land
To ''wreck'' their freight of sunshine on the strand.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Legend of Brittany, i. 33.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To suffer wreck or ruin. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Rocks, whereon greatest men have oftest ''wreck’d.''
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., ii. 228.}}}}

'''wreck<sup>2</sup>†''' (rek), ''v.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wreckage''' (rek′ạ̄j), ''n.''   [< ''wreck''<sup>1</sup> + ''-age''.]   '''1.''' The act of wrecking, or the state of being wrecked.
{{smaller block|''Wreckage'' and dissolution are the appointed issue.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. v. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' That which remains of or from a wreck of any kind; wrecked material in general.
{{smaller block|Only a few years ago, the procession of the fat ox remained, . . . a real piece of ''wreckage'' from vanished civilizations.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXII. 247.}}}}
{{smaller block|Littered above the pavement with the ''wreckage'' and refuse of the market.
{{right|''W. Besant'', Fifty Years Ago, p. 61.}}}}

'''wreck-chart''' (rek′chärt), ''n.'' A chart showing the location and date of wrecks on any coast, as an aid in avoiding them or as a guide in searching for them.

'''wrecker''' (rek′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''wreck''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A person who purposely causes a wreck or wreck-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
